utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Madam Registrar, could you kindly --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. All the accused are here. Same for the Defence teams except for -- yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic is working away from the courtroom for a few days, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls, Mr. Vanderpuye. I don't see anyone else. Mr. -- are there any preliminaries? Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours. There is a preliminary issue with respect to the disclosure of certain documents that I furnished to the Defence relevant to the witness's testimony. The documents are essentially internal documents consisting of information reports, personal notes, notes to file, and things of that nature which were missed during the course of preparing the witness for her testimony. Yesterday, pursuant to the witness's testimony about the transferral of the binder of 500 pages to the Tribunal, I undertook to search for documentation pursuant to the request of my colleague, Mr. Zivanovic. And during the course of that search uncovered a small cache, if you were, or a file, of documents that were apparently prepared by Ms. Frease. And I think that, after having reviewed the documents, it appears that they are directly relevant to the issues upon which she has testified and I have furnished that on to the Defence. At the time I compiled the documents I had e-mailed the Defence and invited them to consider their position with respect to this matter, and I have differing views on how to proceed. So that's the reason why I have raised at this point and I think it would be worthy of some discussion, since Ms. Frease is actually on the stand presently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that information, Mr. Vanderpuye. Would these documents have been -- would these documents be such as would fall under Rule 66 or Rule 68? Could you explain that, please? Because obviously we haven't seen them, we are not aware of the nature of their substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We have reviewed the documents with respect to Rule 68 or any exculpatory material that may be contained in them and, in fact, they are consistent with the witness's testimony and to the extent that they actually bear upon the testimony of previous witnesses, in particular the commander that was referred to, what's contained in the documents is also consistent with the testimony that was offered by that witness. But obviously I'd leave that to the Defence to dispute or accept. The statements are also the statements of the witness. And so I think this they do fall under Rule 66 to that extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. All right. So does any one of the Defence team wish to address this matter? Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: First I would like to allow you to see the complete picture, and I think, although with all due respect, my learned colleague, you -- didn't fill you in on some critical information. We received or an e-mail was sent to us at 12.29 this afternoon telling us it's urgent. There was an invitation. His invitation was to suspend Ms. Frease's testimony. We did not have the documents attached to the e-mail. They were given to us shortly before we entered this courtroom laying our desk here, approximately 2.10, 2.05 for some who came earlier. We've always wanted the complete file of Stefanie Frease; we were never given that complete file. My learned friend says on page 1, line 20, "it's information reports, personal notes, notes to file, and things of that nature." I want them on the record or someone to attest in writing to me that that's her complete file. I dare say that I suggest that it is not, that this individual, Ms. Frease, has been doing this intercept project for several and many years. She's engaged with many researchers, many other investigators, many witnesses. I'd like to get her complete file. It's important. I do not, again with the most respect, rely on the Prosecutor to tell me whether that evidence is consistent or part of Rule 68. I'd like for the benefit of my client to make that examination. They've invited us to suspend Ms. Frease's testimony because it's a critical issue to have a witness testify and give answers. I don't believe that they're consistent, her answers. I don't believe they have been, but we could argue about that at some other time. My other big question to this Court is, the alternative is not necessarily to suspend Ms. Frease's testimony, but it's to strike her testimony. Who is she and what is she? If she is offering summary of data that we can summarise and we can assess, whether it's for its authenticity or reliability, that's the job of the attorneys, I respectfully say, to try to convince the Court and ultimately Your Honour's decision on those issues. All she's doing is an investigator who assisted on a project. If it's fair that a Court will allow an investigator to give such testimony, we also have our investigators and personnel who would like to testify and say, "Here is our analysis, let us testify as to how we see the evidence." I don't think it is fair. She showed us yesterday, I believe at least, that she doesn't have a unique expertise in this area at all, whether it's chain of custody or whether it's on assessment of reliability of these documents. She's admitted she's not a criminologist, said that she did not utilise a forensic expert in part of her testimony yesterday. What is the basis of her testimony? If it's to fill time, I could accept that, I suppose, but it's not expertise in any manner. So we would ask that her testimony be suspended, but only after we receive her entire file so we can have adequate time to review it or, in the alternative, to have her testimony stricken and barred from this Court or this proceeding. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Ostojic. Anyone else wishes to address the Trial Chamber? Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to simply say that I agree with the submission of Mr. Ostojic. After having seen a few documents, a few of these documents, I see that they are internal notes, but also information reports about potential witnesses, and about -- other people were mentioned in other documents and that could be a relevant source of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Just to say that we also join in the arguments presented by Mr. Ostojic and to say that that is on both issues, that is both the issue of the documents that we have just been served with, but also the issue concerning the purpose and the meaning of the testimony of the witness who is presently on the stand. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I first ask you to address this complete file issue that was raised by Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The complete file issue raised by Mr. Ostojic, I think, can be bifurcated. One has to do with the documents that are contained within it that are reasonably discoverable under the Rules and others has to do with documents that are not discoverable but are, in fact, the work product of the witness and of the Office of the Prosecutor. So to the extent that Mr. Ostojic wants everything that Ms. Frease has done, that is contained in this file, I don't know that he's entitled to everything that was created by Ms. Frease for two reasons: One is that some of those materials are internal work product and therefore privileged and not disclosable to the extent that they don't contain exculpatory material. The second is he is entitled to documents that bear -- that have some relevancy to the subject matter of her testimony. Mr. Ostojic indicated previously Ms. Frease has worked with the Office of the Prosecutor for a long time, she worked in different capacities, some of which do not bear upon the subject matter of her testimony or the capacity in which she has been called in this case. So there is a limit with respect to the documents that are relevant to her testimony. As far as I can tell the Court now, the documents that have been disclosed represent -- represent the -- the totality of the documents that we are aware of that bear upon the subject matter of her testimony that are not otherwise privileged and that are not otherwise the subject of a work product within the Office of the Prosecutor. The second portion of Mr. Ostojic's argument, if I may address that, has to do with her capacity to testify in the case. I think the Defence is well aware of the capacity in which Ms. Frease has been called to testify in this matter. We've not represented Ms. Frease to be an expert in relation to her examination or analysis of intercepts. I don't believe that was ever a question asked on direct and I don't think it's ever been implied that she's been called in that capacity. She's testified previously, and I'm sure that the Defence is aware of the subject matter of that testimony, which is essentially consistent with the testimony that she's offered here today with respect to her work concerning the intercepts used in this case. It would seem to me that the appropriate time in which to raise the objection to the propriety of calling Ms. Frease as a Prosecution witness would have been well in advance of her testimony, and as soon as the subject matter of her testimony would reasonably have become known to the Defence, which I could only assume would have preceded actually the commencement -- well, would have shortly followed the commencement of the case, as soon as she was identified on the Prosecution's 65 ter witness list. It seems to me that the objection to her testimony is untimely; it could have been made either at the beginning of her testimony or prior thereto and, in fact, should have been. The second reason that I think it's an inappropriate objection is because Ms. Frease is not testifying in the capacity of an expert, but is testifying about particular work that she did concerning the intercept collection in a manner that would be helpful to the Court in understanding the nature and relation of the intercepts to other material factual questions in the case, such as the -- the -- such as intercepts that have been recorded at multiple sites, identifying for the Court precisely in which instances those communications have occurred because that was not within the ken of the individual intercept operators to do. It was not necessarily clear and immediately identifiable from the examination of the material because there are instances in which those transcriptions occur simultaneously but are designated by different times and different locations such that it wouldn't be readily identifiable to the Court and therefore her testimony is extremely useful in that regard. She's being called in that capacity in order to crystallise for the Court the process by which the intercepts that are being offered by the Prosecution was gathered in order to crystallise for the cord those actions undertaken by the Prosecution or with respect to the intercepts that bear upon the reliability of those intercepts. She was not asked directly what her opinion was, with respect to whether or not the intercepts were reliable. She was asked about specific tasks that she undertook in that regard in order to evaluate the reliability of those -- of that material. So I think that Mr. Ostojic's argument, although I think is well articulated, is -- is not -- is not one upon which Ms. Frease's testimony should be stricken or precluded, particularly as a result of the disclosure of the documents in addition to the propriety of her testimony in the first instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. I have a few questions to you before I give the floor again to Mr. Ostojic and anyone else who wishes to speak. You dealt in the beginning, in response to my invitation about whether the disclosure in relation to Ms. Frease's testimony is complete or not, and you seem to hint, if I understood you well, that disclosure is complete, barring documents which are not subject to disclosure. Do I read you well?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was just momentarily distracted. I'm reading the transcript and I do understand your question. Well, I will say that you read me close to well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So could you make -- could you bring me closer?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll try to draw you in just a little. We are presently continuing to search, to make sure that what we've disclosed is as complete as it can be. The documents that I have disclosed right now are all of the documents that -- that we are aware of that bear on the testimony -- as I've said before, bear on her testimony and are otherwise not privileged from disclosure. Because of the fact that we discovered this at the last instance, I am reluctant to tell the Court or represent that it is an exhaustive list of all of the documents. We have been searching our own files essentially since I -- since before I e-mailed the Defence, and I think that was several hours ago, and these are the documents that we've come up with and identified. I cannot make that representation to the Court, I -- I feel uncomfortable doing it and I don't think it would be genuine to make that representation. But I can tell you that there do exist documents that are, in fact, privileged. So that I don't want to make the representation that there are five documents in the file that we found. They are not, they are more, but those documents, it is our position, are work product, are unrelated otherwise to the subject matter of the witness's testimony, and are -- and are privileged. I think that's about the extent of the representation I can make to the Court and Defence counsel at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And one further question. Obviously none of us has seen these documents from -- but from what I could gather at least, some indication that these are internal memoranda from Ms. Frease to her superiors, I suppose. Wouldn't that fall under paragraph A of Rule 70 which excludes or -- excludes from disclosure, reports, memoranda, or other internal documents prepared by a party's assistance or representatives in connection with the investigation or preparation of a case? Because I heard what Madam Fauveau had to say, I heard what Mr. Ostojic had to say, and what you said, because if that is the case, and you are disclosing them nonetheless, the question that Mr. Ostojic put about the completeness or otherwise of disclosure becomes a little bit more pertinent. Or opens up anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would respond as follows, Mr. President: The view that Mr. McCloskey and our team is taking with respect to these documents is a broad one. We're not seeking in any way to stretch our view the limitations of paragraph A of Rule 70 in order to avoid the disclosure of these documents. We feel that they are pertinent to the subject matter of the witness's testimony, and frankly had I seen these documents when Ms. Frease had first testified, they would have been disclosed at that point because they really do bear upon issues that were raised by -- in the cross-examination, and in the direct testimony to an extent. And that is the view that we've taken and that's the reason why we're disclosing them. We're not suggesting that they clearly outside the scope of Rule 70, paragraph A, but we feel that in an abundance of caution and in fairness to the Defence they should be made aware of these documents and they should have them in order to effectively cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then what about who has already cross-examined the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The other half of the e-mail that I had sent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the sore point of the whole debate because Mr. Zivanovic will ask for another two hours 40 minutes. More. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, I'm trying to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We had considered the complication of attending to the fact that Mr. Zivanovic had already completed his examination, and what one of the Defence counsel has suggested would be perhaps to have Mr. Zivanovic or those who had already proceeded or completed their cross-examinations to review the documents and to the extent that re-cross-examination should be required, we're certainly in a position, I think, to consent to that. Of course that is within the discretion of the Court and there are time considerations and constrains but I think that would be an appropriately reasonable tact to take particularly for Mr. Zivanovic. For counsel that haven't gone yet, then it becomes a question of how much time they would require in order to review the documents. I can tell you there are about five documents and their length, of course, is not necessarily material, but they are not particularly long. But I think it is appropriate for counsel to have the opportunity to review them. I don't know necessarily that that would -- I don't know necessarily that that would change the cross-examination that's already been undertaken thus far. That is entirely up to Defence counsel and I wouldn't presume -- I wouldn't presume to tell them how to do their job or what's important to their clients or them. I think that is a reasonable consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you very much, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Ostojic, since you are in a somewhat different position than that of your colleagues as you are first to go, I would also invite you to address this last point that I raised with Mr. Vanderpuye, and which he has responded to. In other words, being prepared for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As I think the Court has seen, everything can be placed in a certain context. When we discuss issues like completeness of documents or records, we honestly get a respectfully evasive answer. If there is a privilege and if there is a work product privilege that they are asserting, they can make a privilege log, identify the documents as we do in many jurisdictions to tell us how many documents, the Court could have examined that ex parte to determine whether it constitutes either a privilege or work product. They don't go that far. They took a chance on calls Ms. Frease and now they don't want to suffer the consequences of some of her testimony and some of her cross by supplementing with additional and new documents. If they give us one of her internal documents, I say they've -- in themselves have made an admission that all the documents should come in from Ms. Frease. They've waived the right to raise it as a privilege or a work product. Secondly, we've seen the argument in connection with the completeness. Again, I have to stress, it's not complete. It's clear it's in the complete. We think there is more documents than this. There must have been more documents if she interrelated and spoke to many different investigators, researchers, attorneys, et cetera. We're not looking to get behind their strategy, although they've shared that with us and I hope they had. We know what their strategy is in the case and it it's developing slowly and we recognise it. We're not looking for anything internal. We are looking for things to shed light on the two critical issues in connection with the logbooks, that is whether or not they are reliable and whether or not they are authentic. We think from that evidence, from those internal memos, it can draw or shed some light on that issue. In connection with my colleague sharing on page 10 where he says he felt that, that we should have had them in order to effectively cross-examine the witnesses. He's correct on that. It is undisputed in order to cross-examine a witness, especially an in-house witness that the Prosecutor has nurtured, developed, worked with over the course of the last several years, we should have had all that material before. We should have had it not only before her testimony but well before the trial commenced last August or July when it formally did. Finally he raises a claim that Ms. Frease is a fact witness. I will accept his agreement on that, that she's a fact witness, and I would ask the Court to just look at some of the questions that my learned friend asked this witness. He used the word "opinion" many times, several times during his direct examination of her. And just so the record's clear, if we look on Monday's transcript during the direct examination, the 26th of February, page 66: "Question: In evaluating --" lines 13 and 14. "In evaluating the two intercepts, would it be fair to say in your opinion that the summarisation version of the conversation carries the same import as the verbatim version of the intercept." He goes on, on many of these instances, to ask her opinion not only authenticity, but on reliability, on import of -- on the import of certain intercepts, and he knows that it's a violation. Or I should say they know it's a violation. She is not an opinion expert, she shouldn't be allowed to give opinion testimony. I again, as I said in the opening -- in the opening argument on this issue, we should bar her testimony in connection with the opinions that she has given. If she is a fact witness, walk us through the chain of custody, walk us through where you felt there is reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Move to the next point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Those are the three points I'd like to -- it's a very serious issue, but I think it's continuing problem. So on privilege, we should be given a privilege log. Completeness of documents, they have not shared with us and they -- yet they agree that those documents are necessary. They're giving us a selective review of those documents. And number three, it's clear that she's acting as an opinion and fact witness and we ask that you to strike all her opinion testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't answered my last posit to you, namely whether you have had time to go through these documents, whether we can -- we can proceed with her testimony and possibly reopen for you to put further questions afterwards. What's your position on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's a twofold question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that you are a very practical lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's a twofold question, quite candidly. One, I have not reviewed the documents; that's why I thought it was important for the Court to know that we received the e-mail at 12.30 and we received the documents moments after 2.00. So I honestly have not reviewed them at all. I looked at the first page. It's more extensive than just a couple of pages. There's details there that I think are necessary for us to develop and look at so I've not looked at it. I would leave it to the Court's pleasure. I think, though, that it's time that we take a position that if these things keep happening that we will not become practical in every instance and allow the Prosecutor, in my view, to manipulate the process and force our hand by giving us or spoon feeding us documents in order to complete a cross-examination and continuously bring witnesses in. If that were true, then we would invite on every occasion other witnesses to come back. After Ms. Stefanie Frease testifies, the intercept operators -- and try to then join the testimony to see if they are consistent or inconsistent. I think it's not practical to do that, but the more practical solution is what was offered by my learned friend, the invitation to suspend her from testifying today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He never reiterated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's in his -- I read his -- I read his e-mail and I don't that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was in his e-mail to you. He's never stated that in court. So I think we'll -- yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I -- if I may add in answer to the same questions but just to give it -- and maybe in a different -- to answer in a different light. First of all, with the nature of the information that we are provided for, without going into the details, these are documents entitled, "Information report." So they are not work product; they really basically give information as a -- as a witness statement, and we have two information reports. With the same -- as was put to you by my colleague, Mr. Ostojic, we have not had time to review these documents personally on behalf of my client. We are not in a position to proceed today with further cross-examination. But that brings an issue, Mr. President, that we would like to bring forward. We did file a motion some time ago at the beginning of this case asking for an order from the Trial Chamber to order the Prosecution to give us a list of all documents they have for each witness. We never have received such a list. We have received many indexes with lots of material, but never have we received a list of material for each witness. The Trial Chamber decided to deny the motion, and said that the Prosecution was doing its best. I agree, they're doing their best. But doing their best, not having such a list doesn't allow us to maybe in advance query, are you sure you're not missing something with this witness because of our own investigation. We are not a position to do that. Also, in the Trial Chamber's decision - and I couldn't have -- I was looking for the decision now - it also said that should the Prosecution come up with new documents that there would be a delay given to the Defence or some time given to the Defence to prepare before we can cross-examine such a witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Any further comments? None. I think we need to have a short break. We need to discuss a little bit amongst ourselves. It should be a short break rather than a long one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I can put a question to the Prosecution. I think I see a point in Mr. Ostojic's submission. It is related in general to Rule 70(A). If witness is of a kind who's coming from in-house, so called, who worked as an investigator or is working as an investigator or whatever, then the reports, memoranda, or other internal documents may be differently treated from the case of the ordinary witnesses. So for example, internal report or the memoranda produced by or in relation to the witness, can they not be viewed as kind of statements of the witness, previous statements? I wonder whether you followed my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was just reading it on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you would bear with me for just a moment, Your Honour. Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is, does the fact that an investigator becomes a witness make him or her fall out of the parameters of the privilege which is envisaged in Rule 70? This is basically the question that Judge Kwon has put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In particular in light of the words which says, "Notwithstanding the provisions of Rule 66 and 67." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, maybe I can answer it this way: We don't feel that the mere fact that the character of the witness, in other words the capacity in which they are called, necessarily broadens the scope of Rule 70(A). We are disclosing this material because we believe fundamentally that it falls outside the scope of Rule 70(A). And the reason that it falls outside Rule 70(A) is based upon the character of the evidence as opposed to the fact that the witness created it or the capacity in which the witness created it. The material that we've disclosed here bears directly upon the subject matter of this witness's testimony. In other words, every document that she's created for her superior in the capacity of -- in her capacity as an investigator doesn't necessarily warrant disclosure, but warrants disclosure to the extent that it bears materially upon the subject matter of her testimony. That's the reason why we've disclosed it. And I hope that answer your question. I'm sure that you will let me know if it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In case of 66(A)(ii) disclosure, whether the document has any bearing upon the subject matter or relevance, has nothing to do with the duty of the Prosecutor to disclose those.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct. But under Rule 70(A) it seems to me that it creates an exception to the Prosecutor's obligation to disclose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the crux of the matter is, will lie upon the distinction between the statements and the internal documents, whether a certain document should be viewed as statements of the witness, then that should be disclosed. Whether it has the bearing upon the subject matter or not, has nothing to do with the disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I can agree thus far.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think so. My understanding of Rule 70(A), though, is that it is an exception to the disclosure requirements under Rule 66 and that's the reason why it's preceded by the term "notwithstanding," that that obliges -- well, not obliges. But it gives the Prosecutor or the party the opportunity not to disclose the documents even though they would otherwise be required to be disclosed under those Rules. So, yes, I think we agree to that extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to suspend the sitting. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can I make a suggestion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why don't you look at these documents that we've been given? I'm happy for you to. Then you can decide whether those statements -- or mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wouldn't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't mind either. You know that it hasn't been the practice, but sometimes that becomes useful. We haven't asked because no one offered and it's also because our practice is not to be the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we have some extra copies if the Court would like to see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it will help us decide on at least one issue, if to proceed at all today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: One, two, three, four, is this all in -- in order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, can you please show them to Mr. Haynes so that we have a confirmation that we are talking of the same entire collection of documents. It's not a question of mistrust, please don't -- don't misunderstand me. More of a formality than anything else. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have had the opportunity to look at these documents and I would like to inform the Chamber that there is at least one document amongst the documents that was disclosed to us as a document that falls under the scope of Rule 68. It clearly falls under the scope of that rule, Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know, but we are going to see the documents. Which of these documents are you referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the -- [In English] Information report submitted, Stefanie Frease, source -- [Interpretation] I won't tell you the source. It's an officer from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you have to say about that, Mr. Vanderpuye, if you can detect -- identify the document Madam Fauveau is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm -- I'm not sure if I have identified the document that my colleague is referring to, and maybe she could be a little bit more precise so I can -- I can see what she's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have the date of the document or the first three words or four words of the text?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a document dated the 24th of April, 1998. There is no ERN number on that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So as stated we need to suspend the sitting. We will be coming back to you shortly. Thank you. --- Break taken at 2.54 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, allow me to start from here. We have been informed that while we were deliberating the accused have not had time to leave the courtroom and have their break. So we have already discussed that and we will come to a break soon to allow you to have a short break. I'll try to deal with the various issues that have been raised that, in our opinion, require to be dealt with. First point that was raised by Mr. Ostojic and on which we heard submissions from other Defence teams as well as from Mr. Vanderpuye, which we have taken note of, we have the following: We have noted in particular the statement made by Mr. Vanderpuye, namely, or to wit that further searches are ongoing to ensure that disclosure in relation to this witness is complete. Now, the Trial Chamber cannot fail to point out that failure to disclose material under Rule 66(A)(ii) in a timely fashion can, as has been shown in other cases, lead to undesired and undesirable consequences which include frustration of proceedings and, many a time, extra costs, expenses, for the Tribunal. Because of this, but not only because of this, the Trial Chamber cannot condone this and has no doubt that the material in question should have been disclosed earlier. The Trial Chamber also acknowledges that the disclosure of the material in question at this particular stage of the proceedings, when the witness has not yet finished her testimony, and when cross-examination by almost all the Defence teams is not yet concluded, allows for the rights of the accused to be protected and to be protected in a timely fashion and minimises the frustration of the proceedings. The Trial Chamber agrees further that the late disclosure of the material in question entitles the Defence teams to ask for a suspension of the proceedings in order that they may examine this material and prepare their cross-examination. We are, therefore, prepared to grant any additional -- to grant any additional time as required, accordingly. This will include, of course, the Popovic Defence team, if they wish to further cross-examine the witness. Finally, we see absolutely no merit to the submission of the Beara, Nikolic and Miletic Defence teams to strike the testimony of the witness. Our order is to proceed with her testimony subject to what we have decided before. What I suggest now is we will have a 25-minute break so that the -- or 20-minute break so that the accused can have time to relax a little bit - 20 minutes - after which we will call on each one of you to see whether you wish to postpone your cross-examination until some other time or whether you wish to proceed today and maybe come back with further questions at a later stage. This we will leave in your hands and we'll deal with it after the break. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe I suggest if we could ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. In addition to what I said, perhaps if there is any of the Defence teams, if there is any of the Defence teams that can give us feedback now before the break, then perhaps it will be more useful for us to be able to prepare better for the remaining time that we have today. Yes, I noticed you standing, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was just about to suggest that maybe the Defence teams, we could provide you right away with our submissions in this regard so that we can address maybe what we do if we cannot proceed today. On behalf of the Accused Drago Nikolic we will not be prepared to continue cross-examination today but we could be ready the first opportunity tomorrow. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I start with you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've tried to look at the documents and I haven't had a chance obviously to review them in detail. We would prefer not to proceed. I mean, we are ready, as I think the Court noted yesterday, to ask further questions of her. They might end up being inconsistent with some of the things she may or may not have said. But I think it would be more practical to not proceed now, to suspend it for a matter of days, whatever the Court's desire is, and bring her back after we've had an opportunity to digest the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Does the Borovcanin Defence team wish to address the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we've announced that we will not ask any questions of this witness, and the discussion of today does not change our position in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. I-- that's why I wanted to ask you in any case, because it could have changed your position. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just -- we're not getting the transcript on the screen, so we're trying to follow it, both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am having it. So are my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mine stops on page 22, line 8, in the middle of Mr. Bourgon's discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, can -- can we proceed and you check on -- the transcript on the other monitor, maybe? And then we'll soon be having a break and we will look into the matter. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would rather consult the documents and cross-examine the witness later tomorrow. We would be ready tomorrow for this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be lying if I was to suggest to the Court that these documents are going to make any profound difference to my cross-examination. I am confident they are not going to make any difference; however, I am anxious to maintain our position of, in effect, going after my learned friends. It was something we had agreed with them and it is a position we would like to maintain. I am bound to say the cross-examination will be about 20 minutes in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and I thank you also for the approach you take, which I can assure you the Trial Chamber will respect because -- yeah, anyway, I will not say anything further. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: As I think the Chamber knows, we don't propose to cross-examine Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But your position remains the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So I think we'll have a break. But before we do so, I would like to know what do you propose to do if we suspend the testimony of Ms. Frease until a later time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's what I was going to raise, Your Honours. PW-104 is in the waiting-room and he's been there for a couple of hours. So if he is not going to start today, I would like to release him rather than keep him waiting. I -- I have -- I haven't personally received it, but I have been told there was an e-mail from Mr. Meek that strenuously objected to him going forward today, and in all fairness to the Defence, they expected a delay because they thought that Ms. Frease would continue, and I -- I believe Ms. Fauveau also said that she did not want any other witnesses going forward. So I think the Defence position is that they are not ready for another witness, and -- we are ready, but if that's the case and as I say, I can understand it, then I would rather release him as soon as possible rather than hold him longer in that room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long is his testimony expected to last in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say exactly, but I think about an hour or around a session. An hour, depending on how it goes. Not too long. Not hours and hours, so they would reach him today. But I think their position was that they did not want him to start because they're just not prepared for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see two possible options, without committing, of course, the Trial Chamber. If PW-104 starts today, will he be cross-examined -- not today, but tomorrow, that means Ms. Frease's suspension of her testimony will out -- last a good part of tomorrow or maybe the entire of tomorrow. Or if we decide to proceed with PW-104's testimony in chief only today, does that mean, or does that entail that he will return for cross-examination when the cross-examination of Ms. Frease has been concluded? I would like to hear comments or -- on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's a difficulty I would like to avoid. Both -- mainly for the witness's sake, but also for logistical reasons. Without getting into it in open session, the witness is quite nervous, or was when I saw him a couple days ago, does not feel particularly good, and I would rather not prolong and put gaps in his testimony in requiring him to come back at some other time. So for that reason -- just prefer that for the witness's sake I would rather start and continue and have him finish in one block and have it over with, but otherwise, depending on the Court's decision, it would impact on when he is available. I can't remember the estimate, but I think there is a significant amount of cross-examination anticipated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think five hours. Five hours, and there are still about another five hours left for Stefanie Frease. So I think we will have a break now. We need to discuss further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would it be acceptable to the Defence teams if you start the cross-examination of PW-104 tomorrow? That would mean you will acquire more time in relation to Stefanie Frease. Yeah, yeah, we'll hear the direct today, obviously. And then we continue -- we start -- there won't be any cross-examinations today, unless someone wishes to go ahead. And we'll have the cross-examinations tomorrow so that we can send this man home before the weekend. Agreed? Agreed? All right. I think -- so we will have the 20-minute break that we promised you, and we'll come back -- first I need to explain to Ms. Frease, please. So ask her to show in -- for her to come in for a short explanation. Yeah, but they cannot explain to her. You will? All right. Okay. Thank you. So we will have PW-104. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. If Ms. -- if Ms. Frease is not going to come back in the courtroom, I would like to make sure that because we have new documents, that there will not be any communications between the Prosecution and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then bring her at the beginning of the next session and I will explain to her. We can bring her right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I regret to inform you that we will not proceed with your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And at least for the most part of tomorrow. There has arisen a procedural matter that we had to deal with. And because of that we are going to proceed with the testimony of someone else and then continue the cross-examinations at a -- your cross-examination afterwards. In the meantime it's my responsibility to draw your attention that you are still in the process of testifying, and that you are not to discuss or allow the Prosecution to discuss with you matters related to your -- to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose you know the procedure and that should be clear enough for you. I also wanted to apologise to you for having kept you waiting for over two hours, not knowing what's happening. I suppose in due course you will become aware of the problems that we have had, and the reason why we had to postpone your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, I understand you wish to address the Chamber before the next witness is ushered in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With all due respect, we would like to make a record and preserve the record. We have a motion to bar the testimony of this witness on several grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: This upcoming witness, 104. Your Honour, this interview of this witness - if you don't know this, it will come out if you don't grant this motion - the interview conducted with this witness breached all of the OTP's very own internal procedures in conducting interviews. In every interview that is tape-recorded they always say when they take a break, "We won't talk about the case." We come back in -- they go on the record and they say, "We haven't talked about the case." That's their internal policy. In this case the interviewer, the attorney and the investigator took a break, we don't know what happened outside that break, it's not on the record. The witness was brought back in, and then all of the sudden the witness was asked questions changing his prior -- previous testimony, the statement he had previously given. We don't know what happened with that. We do know that this witness had to have been known by the OTP at least as early as 2000, because that was when the Zvornik Brigade documents were received. Again, we have no information whatsoever as to what was said outside the interview, the technical interview, violating all the rules of the OTP. We ask the testimony be barred on that grounds. If not, Your Honours, we ask that this witness must be read his rights, that he does have a right to a lawyer, et cetera. Further, Your Honours, we would ask you to -- we brought this up before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What -- what right are you referring to? That -- as -- as --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: His rights as a suspect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Then the right as a suspect that does not entitle him to have a lawyer here present while he is giving testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No. No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we have on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The reason, Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "If not, Your Honour, we ask that this witness must be read his rights that he does have a right to a lawyer," et cetera. Of course if we ask that we caution him in terms of Rule 90, we will do so. We will do that with every -- every witness that becomes necessary, when it becomes necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's what we request, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Secondly, Your Honour, we ask you -- we have raised this before, and for the record we're going to raise it again. We ask this Trial Chamber to effectively entertain a judicial estoppel. The Prosecutors in this case are taking an inconsistent position from a former proceeding, and that is Blagojevic and Jokic. This inconsistency, we believe, undermines the fairness of the trial and violates our client's right to judicial process, fundamentally violating his right to a fair trial. In Blagojevic and Jokic, the same Prosecution team with the same facts said security was not involved. They didn't hold a candle, they had no command, no nothing. Now we have just the opposite. We have an inconsistent position, it's inconsistent, Judge, and basically the bottom line, and we're not saying necessarily bad faith even has to come in the picture. The bad faith shouldn't be a condition. The reason we ask for judicial estoppel is because if you don't, Judge, it's just going to corrupt the judicial process. It's not right. They can't go in one case, same facts, and say one thing, and then come along here in this case and say something completely inconsistent. So on those two grounds, Judge, we ask that this witness's testimony be barred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek. Who is going to respond to that? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I can respond to the -- I think what he's called the estoppel theory first, is it's an issue that involves the Blagojevic case and I will respond to it briefly. Something of this kind of potential, import, and significance based on the record of a previous case really should not be -- again, I am a broken record on this, it should not be brought up at the last minute like this, though -- but I can respond. First of all, the simplest response is that there is no inconsistency. I, nor the Prosecution in the previous case, no one ever suggested security was not involved. Security has always been the -- the -- in the theme of -- in the theme and theory of the case has always been the people that were on the ground coordinating, organising, and facilitating the -- the detention, the transportation, and the execution of this case. Now, as I have been in other cases involving commanders, General Krstic, Blagojevic, Obrenovic, the Defences of those commanders has always been: These security officers have done this on their own acting under their own chain of command outside of my authority. And my arguments have been very briefly that a security officer is not a commander. A security officer is only empowered to act under the orders of his commander. And therefore, I think Mr. Ostojic's favourite quote of mine is that Beara is an empty vessel, which is true, until he is filled with the orders of his commander, General Mladic, and then he takes on his role as a security officer, dealing with the military police, dealing with prisoners. And this has always been the case, and we have never suggested security officers are not involved. I took a plea from Momir Nikolic who admitted his guilt in -- in -- in this case, and he was a security officer, and his testimony in this courtroom as to the involvement of other security officers. I mean, I don't know where they're getting this. It can be dealt with fairly quickly, but again these sorts of broad claims like this, I think it would be better had they -- they been something that we have a little bit of notice of. I can respond to this one easily, as I can with most of them. But I think in the future it would be better if we had a little more preparation for this sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What about the first point raised by Mr. Meek in relation to the statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can respond to that, Your Honour. Mr. Meek's representations are completely inaccurate in several respects. This was a witness interview held in -- in Zvornik. At one point we did take a break, and the witness answered some questions off of the tape, because he was not willing to go on, on tape. The -- an information report was written up immediately that night, explaining exactly what happened and why. The witness at no time changed any of his testimony, and there is a record of exactly what happened during the break. In addition, the next day -- not immediately after, but two days -- the second day following the initial interview, I met the witness again somewhere else and went on tape in order to put on tape, on the record, exactly what had happened. Now, there is no inconsistency, I would suggest, in anything the witness has said. What the witness said before we went off tape, in answer to some questions that I can't specify here in open session, is that I can't speak about that. I can't talk about that. I'm not willing to talk about that. I have that interview in Sanction. I'm very happy to play that for Your Honours so Your Honours can hear the witness's voice and hear the way he felt at that time. They can cross-examine the witness about what happened, and we didn't violate any policy. If a witness at this point is unable or scared to go on and then we -- we memoralise it in writing as a way any written statement would be, there is no prejudice whatsoever. And, as I said, I did everything I could to make it very clear. I wrote an information report immediately saying why we had taken the break and what happened during the break. And then I met the witness again to confirm on tape that that information report was accurate. And they have all of that, they've had it for three months. Now, if he may be saying again well, I don't trust you, I think you lied in your information report, that's another thing. But then that's something he can follow up in his cross-examination of the witness. But certainly none of it would rise to the extraordinary remedy of barring probative evidence. And I think when the witness testifies you will see that he was not inconsistent and I will move to put in the interview, the information report and the subsequent interview in order to rebut these challenges which have been made against me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you sit down, Mr. Nicholls, do you wish to take a position about the third proposition of the Beara Defence team, namely that we should caution this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, I don't -- I don't object to a caution. I -- this is a -- this was a witness, not a suspect interview. I don't -- I don't think a caution is strictly necessary in this case. I don't see where they see it in his interview, because the substance, without saying what I can -- can we go into private session for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are back in open session. We have three issues that we have to decide upon that have been raised by Mr. Meek and responded to by Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Nicholls respectively. We will take them one by one. The first one is to strike off the statement of this witness on the basis that it was irregularly taken, to wit in contravention of the internal rules of the Office of the Prosecutor. We have heard the parties' submissions on the issue. We believe this matter can be dealt with by the parties either during examination-in-chief or cross-examination or both. And we would then be in a position to evaluate better the suggestion or the submission of the Beara Defence team accordingly. The second submission as regards estoppel, we do not see a nexus with the testimony of this particular witness a priori, so there we do not see a reason why the submission that you have made, Mr. Meek, and which you can proceed with in the course of this trial, as we go along, should serve as a reason why this witness in particular should come into course and bring in turn an estoppel as we know it. The third matter that you raised is whether we should grant -- we should caution the witness before he starts giving evidence as to his position or rights under Rule 90 out of an abundance of caution, not knowing exactly the details because we are not provided with the statement beforehand, we will do so after he has been sworn in. We will caution him accordingly. Any further matters you would like to raise in relation to this witness before he comes in? Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just like to -- I know my colleague requested that the witness be given a caution or rights. But I think what we are discussing here, when we look under Rule 90, I don't think it should be regarded as a caution. In other cases, in many respects, whenever a witness comes in and one of the parties believes it is a good procedure to remind the witness that he may refuse to answer and then that he may be forced to answer by the Trial Chamber with the consequence that whatever he says could not be used in other proceedings, some Trial Chambers have used this in the past in giving this type of information to all witnesses appearing before them. So I would like to avoid that we consider this being a caution or a legal caution in any way. It's information we give to witnesses about the procedure and how they will testify. Now, we will recall with the last witness I made a request under Rule 91 Alpha about the witness being reminded about his right to tell the truth. Now, that's -- this for me has a legal connotation, but the first one not. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I prefer not to comment on that and proceed and not waste time on this. Let's bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. And welcome to this Tribunal. We are about to start with your testimony. Madam Usher is going to hand to you the text of a solemn declaration that you are required to make by our Rules, namely to testify the truth. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. We can draw the curtains up. Let me explain to you briefly a few matters. Mr. Nicholls will be putting some questions to you. We have been asked to grant you some protective measures, namely the use of a pseudonym and also facial distortion. I trust these have been explained to you. We have granted these provisional -- these protective measures and we want to hear from you whether they are to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also, at some points in time during your testimony, we will go in private session, the whole exercise being to try our best to hide your identity from the public. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I will say that quite a bit of my direct I will be requesting private session. Because of the testimony. First thing, could I hand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just before you start. Now, I don't know what the substance of your testimony is going to be, sir. But it is my duty to explain to you a right that you have not to incriminate yourself. This is a limited right; it's not an absolute right in our Tribunal. What we have laid down in our rules is that a witness may object to making a statement which might tend to incriminate him. So you have a right, you would have a right to object to answer one or more questions that are put to you. If you do so, however, we have the discretion to compel you to answer the question. We may exempt you from answering the question, but we can ask you to answer it. If we compel you to answer a question, you have a guarantee under our Rules that your testimony and reply to those questions will not be used as evidence in a subsequent possible prosecution against you for any offence except if we catch you giving false testimony. Do you understand the import of what I have explained to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I think we can safely proceed now. Mr. Nicholls, he's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. First, if I could hand the witness - excuse me - the pseudonym sheet which is P02457.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I will ask you to please look at that, read it quietly to yourself, don't read the name on it out loud, but could you please confirm to Their Honours that your name is printed on that sheet of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could that be shown to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the other thing I want to do, sir, is apologise to you, that you have been waiting for, I think, well over two hours in a little room. I want you to know we were -- as I told you, that sometimes happens when the lawyers are arguing about matters that have nothing to do the next witness coming up, it had nothing really to do with your testimony. For the most part we had problems talking about an earlier witness, and I'm sorry that you had to wait so long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please, for the preliminary stuff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At this time period that I have identified for you, can you tell me about any contact you had with officers from the Zvornik Brigade? We are now in open session, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you tell me if you had any contact, any meetings with members of the Zvornik Brigade or other VRS officers at this time, directly before you did what you have described doing in private session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104
utterances.text: Both with the officers of the Zvornik Brigade as well as with some other officers. I did have contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell me where that occurred, which physical location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104
utterances.text: With the Zvornik Brigade officers, I had contacts in my own office in the municipality building. As for the other officers that I had contacts with, those took place in the barracks of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. What I'm asking you about is the contact, the meeting you had in the barracks of the Zvornik Brigade at this time, right after the fall of Srebrenica. Tell me who was present at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104
utterances.text: I can't remember who was present, which officers of the Zvornik Brigade were present. I know that I was there, as well as the officer who introduced himself as Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this officer who -- how did you come to be at this meeting at the Zvornik Brigade where an officer introduced himself as Colonel Beara, why did you go to the Zvornik Brigade to attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104
utterances.text: I went to the Zvornik Brigade every time I was invited there. On that particular occasion I had been invited but I can't remember who invited me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. If you remember, approximately what time of day was it when you were -- when Colonel Beara introduced himself to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104
utterances.text: No, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In your own words, I want you to describe to me and to Their Honours exactly what took place during this meeting at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters, and in particular what you remember Colonel Beara saying. Take your time, think carefully, and just tell me what was said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104
utterances.text: It was not a meeting with an agenda, a protocol or meeting. It looked more like a briefing; we were all standing, we never sat down. As I arrived in the barracks I asked whether Colonel Pandurevic was there, and I was told that he wasn't. I went into a room where I was met by Colonel Beara, and he delivered a brief speech, a monologue which went like this: "We have a lot of prisoners and it is very hard for us to control them. They are at various locations in the Zvornik municipality. We have to get rid of them. I expect assistance from the municipality." I was surprised. I didn't say anything. He then said that he was in command of the barracks and that I should obey his orders. That was more or less that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And specifically when Colonel Beara said we have to get rid of these prisoners, how did he say they were going to get rid of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you - think carefully - what did Beara say was going to happen to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: This question has been asked and answered two times now, and I don't understand if the Prosecutor doesn't like the answer, but this is becoming redundant. This is the second time this question has been asked and answered and I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have -- do you wish to respond to that, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, the -- the answer before was get -- they had to get rid of the prisoners. I want to make sure there is no problem with the translation that's -- and that he cannot give a more complete answer because he, in the past has explained that in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: First off, Judge, first off, Judge, I object -- I really do object to him giving a talking argument, a speaking argument in front of this witness while the witness has got headphones on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek. Stop, Mr. Nicholls. Let's discuss -- let's confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Our position is the following: If you look at page 45, line 5, please. The question that Mr. Nicholls put to the witness was, "And specifically when Colonel Beara said we have to get rid of those -- these prisoners, how did he say they were going to get rid of them?" And the answer that we have in the transcript is "no." Which in itself is almost unintelligible because it does not answer the question. Then we have a second question, which our opinion is that it shouldn't be put. What should -- the way we should proceed is to ask the same question that you asked before to which he answered "no" and the witness will explain exactly what he meant to say, because "no" as such to that question doesn't make sense. It doesn't follow the question. Because the question was, how did he say they were going to get rid of them. So we stick to that question, no further questions on -- on the -- on the issue. He needs to explain his -- his answer. Or complete it anyway. Because I don't know whether it's a question of a wrong transcript or translation or whatever. So, Witness, let me take you in my hands on this. Mr. Nicholls asked you: "When Colonel Beara said, 'We have to get rid of these prisoners,' how did he say they were going to get rid of them?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The colonel said, "We have to get rid of them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he also said that he expected our help in taking care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the question was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, in burying the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. He's back in your hands, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did Colonel Beara say who gave him the order to get rid of the prisoners in such a way that all of their bodies would need to be buried? Did he tell you who gave him that order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104
utterances.text: Yes, he said that that order was from two presidents. I did not ask him. I did not ask any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. For the record, the -- Mr. Nicholls for the Prosecution has concluded his examination-in-chief. One moment, we need to confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just in case, is there any of the Defence teams that is in a position and wishes to start the cross-examination of the witness today? Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, but I'd like to inform you that we will have no questions for the witness. The Defence of General Miletic won't have any questions to put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Madam Fauveau. So I saw you switching on and then switching off your mic. All right. So, sir, unfortunately the way things happened today, which have got nothing to do -- to deal with you, they were procedural issues related to something completely different, has made it necessary to start with your witness [sic] today, which was unexpected. None of the Defence teams expected us to start with your witness [sic] today. We were supposed to start with it tomorrow. Or perhaps even -- even later. The result is that we have a responsibility towards everyone here, Prosecution and Defence, and we will need to give the Defence time in order to prepare for their cross-examination, which will happen tomorrow. So tomorrow we hope to be able to finish with your testimony. It should be possible. And after that you will be free to go home. I hope you understand, and that you understand and accept this. Okay. I take it that he has understood what I said. Sir, we'll see you again tomorrow afternoon at 2.15, and we hope to conclude your testimony then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nicholls, we'll try to utilise some of the time profitably. You will recall Witness 157, if I've got the number right. Now, his testimony or his previous statement was admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis or -- I think it was 92 bis, together with a series of documents, and that was part of our decision, date of which escapes me at the moment. There were, however -- and in our decision we had intimated this, that there were other documents that were not introduced with that witness in that other case, but had been made use of in the course of his testimony. Those couldn't be introduced in the records of this case, pursuant to Rule 92 bis, because they weren't being offered. We had pointed this out to you, and it must have left an impression on you because later on you provided everyone, including ourselves, with a dossier containing these few documents. Leaving them in a state of limbo, we don't know whether you are tendering them or whether you are not tendering them. I think I can be more precise by going straight to the details, if you require me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think I can respond, Your Honour. I'm prepared to. What I provided the Court on 16 of February, and I believe this is a 92 ter witness, I stand to be corrected, but was a chart showing the exhibits which had gone in with his testimony in Krstic and the corresponding exhibits and 65 ter numbers for the exhibits which had been tendered either through him or through other witnesses in this case. What it boils down to is there were two exhibits in Krstic which have not been introduced in this case with 65 ter numbers; those were P331 and P336, the Krstic numbers. Those were the only two at issue, and as Your Honours rightly pointed out, it might be difficult to follow the transcript without having those exhibits, because you wouldn't know what was being referred to. Very briefly, the reason this arose is because all of the other 92 ter witnesses started out at 92 bis and therefore all of their transcripts had been -- all of their exhibits from the previous testimony had been put in as part of the package. This one was converted at a later date in an effort to save time. As regards P331 and 336, I would tender those, but only for the -- for the limited purpose as an aide to follow in the transcript, not for the substance of those exhibits. Now, in fact, I checked the transcript, and -- and all the witness in his Krstic testimony says is, "Yes, that's an intercept," and he gives the date. He authenticates these two documents which we have not put in, in our case. There is a specific procedure we followed for putting in intercepts in this case and for tendering them subject that they would be admitted later after we finish with Ms. Frease. So I am -- and I apologise for not being clearer in the filing on the 16th of February. But those two exhibits are being tendered for the limited purpose of allowing the Trial Chamber to follow exactly what was being discussed in the Krstic testimony. I hope that's reasonably clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Does anyone of the Defence teams wish to comment on this? We hear none. I think we can close it there, leave it there. One moment. I will make a note of it. So the position is we have to adjourn today for reasons well known to you already. We will take up this witness tomorrow again. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have one unrelated point I could raise, Your Honours. During the testimony of PW-101, if you will recall Mr. Bourgon used in his cross-examination statements of unknown persons -- or not statements, I don't know if they were statements, notes, whatever, but he -- information from unknown persons that are unknown to me, perhaps unknown to the Court. And the -- the reason I think given was that there was going to be a request for protective measures or something like that. So, as I recall, Your Honours took that under advisement and I wondered if that's something we could discuss, because I'm still very eager to know who said those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We have of course been discussing that, and you can't even imagine at what lengths. And we will continue discussing amongst ourselves that issue and as it relates to other issues, and our intention was precisely to come back to you to give you a direction on how this and such like incidents in the future will be regulated and how you have to regulate yourselves. So expect us to come forth. What comes as a surprise is that you wish to address us on the merit of -- of -- because, as I remember, at the time you did make some -- some submissions and even acknowledged some matters like you don't want, and you do not pretend to have this and that from -- from Mr. Bourgon. So we were acting under the assumption that this matter had been dealt with by you. But of course if you wish, and anyone else for that matter, from the Defence teams, to make submissions on this, we can meet in 15 minutes' time or 20 minutes' time and -- or now, and have submissions. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Bourgon will excuse me, at the time that my learned friend Mr. Bourgon and my learned friend Mr. Nicholls were having this argument in front of Your Honours, I thought of intervening but chose not to because it seemed to me that it was really a matter between them and at that time it wouldn't be appropriate. It's of course a few days now, but I remember one thought that crossed my mind in relation to what Mr. Nicholls was saying is where in the Rules was he saying that it was incumbent on the Defence to provide the material that he was inviting Mr. Bourgon to provide? And perhaps I could raise that issue now. One other thing, and that's this: It is a matter that may be of concern to other members of the Defence bar, as well as clearly of concern to the Prosecution. If the Chamber can in some way guide us as to what is going through the Chamber's minds, then that might be of real help in submissions that we might want to make. I think the point I'm trying to make is it is not just a matter of interest to Mr. Bourgon, it's of interest to many of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
