utterances.text: And I couldn't agree more, Mr. Josse, and I thank you so much for that intervention, because more or less it reflects the concerns that we have. The feeling actually that we have, that generally speaking, let me not be particular, there is a need for some guidance, and what we had in mind is to provide you with that guidance. Now we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I said earlier on, we attach to these issues great importance, and, since the approach has varied from one Defence team to the other, we became convinced all the more that we need to direct you on this for the duration of the rest of -- of the case. So we'll be coming back to you, but we would like to know, because we were labouring under a different presumption, whether any one of you would either like to make oral submissions or written submissions. We don't have a motion as such. In other words, we -- we had a submission made by Mr. Bourgon at some point in time to which you responded, and to which he again responded, and after which, or in the wake of which we told you we'll come back to you on this and give you a more or less direction. But in the course of our discussions, of course we realised that it is -- you broaden it up and it touches on what one should put to a -- a witness and -- and in cross-examination and in what manner. So the two are related and our intention was to come back to you on everything. If there are -- yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to join with my colleague has said just, Mr. Josse, concerning what exactly the Trial Chamber is looking for in terms of submissions. As far as I am concerned, during the cross-examination of this particular witness I mentioned the fact, and I will simply say over what I said then, which is if I have information in my possession, it must be put to the witness and I can do so as long as I have a reasonable basis, I have a foundation to put some information that exists, I have a duty to put it to the witness. And I also said that I do not feel any obligation whatsoever to inform the Prosecution of this information unless I have a document that I intend to use during cross-examination. And that was the extent of my submission. Now, I see that from what Mr. President, you just mentioned, about how information or questions should be put to the witness during cross-examination, I think that's a different topic. For this reason, I would appreciate if you could -- as was suggested by my colleague, Mr. Josse, if the Trial Chamber can come up with a clear question, is the question what the Defence should give in advance of cross-examination to the Prosecution, or is the question, how should information in the possession of the Defence be placed to a witness during cross-examination? I think these are two very different matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, they are different but related.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would be very glad to answer those matters, whether in writing or orally, as long as we know what exactly is the issue that we are talking about. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will be coming back to you on -- on this. Yes, I see Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just on a related matter, Mr. President, I've asked Defence counsel this, but if -- I would remind them of their obligations to inform us of any alibi evidence that they intend to lead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we -- there is one decision that we handed down in the early stages of the case that that would -- dealt with ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We haven't heard of any evidence -- there may have been one response roughly related to alibi but I heard anything about what Defence is suggesting, for example whether Drago Nikolic is at the Orahovac school or whether Drago Nikolic is at the execution site. We have heard evidence or information I should say, not evidence, that there is a person that drove a truck and took the boy from the -- from the execution site to -- took away. Is that person also suggesting I -- I would imagine, that Drago Nikolic was not at the execution site. If so, I think that's an alibi. So we have not really heard anything regarding alibis. We haven't pushed it. I occasionally make reminders, but we've also -- we've seen Colonel Beara has now been put at the Standard barracks and I'm not sure I've heard -- my recollection may be refreshed but I'm not sure anyone has told me whether there is any alibi or -- regarding Colonel Beara as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I really don't know why my colleague keeps on raising the issue of special defence or alibi. He knows what alibi is. He knows that he has charged his case on the basis of a joint criminal enterprise. He has had answers at least from the Defence of our client. I believe he has also had answers from the others and there is no point of coming back to the issue of alibi over and over again. We have a defence, we are leading this defence, we are answering the case they are leading, and we should not -- stop speaking about alibi. Whether somebody is present at one site or another site or another site, that would not make it an alibi. It would make it part of our defence and has nothing to do that we will lead that evidence as the Prosecution leads its case, we are answering the case and we will do so in our defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Don't expect us to comment on that at this point for sure. Do you wish to address the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm standing Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- or to remain silent?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just want because when they mention our client, you know, and I do object to his categorisation of what alibi is and the manner in which he suggests that the Defence should put on their case. I think we can sit here and argue about it. I'm sure in due course we will have the opportunity before Your Honours. But he shouldn't shape the evidence for you now. His own witnesses are inconsistent as to time, and where any of the defendants or accused have been. So let him address that, why he has those internal inconsistencies. But for him to constantly come up and to try and shape that evidence, I think it's inappropriate. And I will continue to object and stand up and at least pursue my record on that issue. If the Court's concluded that he has met his burden of proof on any of those issues, then the Court should advise us of that and we then can proceed with the Defence case. But I don't think it's there yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We appreciate counsel standing up for their client but it's my position, and perhaps we have to make a filing on it, but if during their Defence they argue that Colonel Beara was not at the Standard factory at the 14 or 15 July, that's an alibi that he's somewhere else. Same thing with Drago Nikolic, is he not at the Orahovac school on the night of the 13th, the day of the 14th, not at the execution site but somewhere else. If that is part of the defence, we need to hear it now under these rules. Perhaps not the rules which we grew up and we practiced in most of our lives, but in these Rules in this court, they have to tell us. And I will file a motion to that respect, so we have differing views on what an alibi is, and I respect that, but I think perhaps we need your guidance from our motions to -- so we can come together on that agreement and then I'm sure Mr. Bourgon and I and the rest of the Defence will agree with your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, [Microphone not activated]. The client we represent here is not being accused for being present at such and such a place at such and such a date. He is being accused because the Prosecution believe that he is come kind of a participant in the joint criminal enterprise. We are -- our case we will address -- as the evidence is being led by the Prosecution, we will address every single step of our Defence as the evidence is being led. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can close on that. Don't expect any one of us to say one single -- one single word more on this than we have said. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have spent a lot of time trying to be as specific as we can in this indictment and what we have mentioned at Orahovac is very specific. We will put this in a motion so that you can rule on it, but if under their theory of an alibi it's just joint criminal enterprise, then there is no alibi. And we have put all the specificity for Orahovac and the other sites for nothing. But probably enough said, we will get in a motion and see from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Is there any -- are there any further submissions on this or on other matters? Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. An unrelated matter. My colleague suggested later on that the next witness could not be Ms. Frease after 104. I would like to know who the next witness is after 104.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is news to me. You heard me address Ms. Frease. My understanding was we finish with 104 and then we continue with Ms. Frease. That's what I -- that's how I understood it. I don't know if any of my colleagues understood it differently. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are of course always discussing things and as items change or may change, I -- as you might add -- I'm going to call Mr. Vanderpuye after this closes and see if -- if there is any more material that has been found. Unfortunately sometimes when we find that there has been a gap in our -- in our review, that gap sometimes opens up into other things, and this is a recent gap, as you know, and I need to go look and see if there is anything else and, of course, if there is, we need it get that to the Defence and -- and if we need to put off Ms. Frease, longer because of that, there is a lot of ifs in there, but that's -- I always am thinking unfortunately in the negative. I'm -- I'm worried that there's more out there and -- but we're really getting on it and it will get resolved quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps you will be in a position to inform the Trial Chamber better tomorrow. The thing is, our concern is that if we start with a different witness after 104, it's our interest to make sure that the Defence teams are prepared. In other words, are given sufficient, timely notice for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The order remains the same, and everyone's been on notice of that order, and -- and they are all here and we have a whole crew that's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My understanding is today would have been taken entirely by Ms. Frease, a good part of tomorrow, then 104 would have come and finished on Friday, and that would have been it and we would be talking of next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As it is, you're suggesting that tomorrow if we finish with this witness by I don't know, 5.30, then you have another witness starting? What I want to make sure is that the Defence are prepared, because we'll have the same problems as we encountered today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour, but I -- and I know and as we appreciate, if there's four documents back there, the Defence may not want to start with -- with Frease, and we understand that and -- and we take responsibility for that. But that's -- again, let's -- that's a hypothetical, let's see where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear what Mr. Bourgon wishes to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we mentioned earlier we are ready to proceed with Ms. Frease tomorrow. The issue is we have one of my colleagues has indicated that she will not have any questions for 104, there is a good chance that we will have another witness after 104 tomorrow. We would just like to know who it is so we can be ready. Whether it is Ms. Frease or the next one, we would like to be told at least one day in advance who we have to prepare for tomorrow. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you have more time than you would have otherwise had to discuss this amongst yourselves and come to a conclusion, because we will have no further business to transact today, things being where they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Except for one last issue. Yesterday you stood up and promised us a response to the Prosecution motion to convert next -- one of the next witnesses to a 92 ter witness, Mr. Bourgon. And I see that Mr. Haynes is going to address that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. In relation to that witness who has previously testified in the Blagojevic case, I don't think any of us have any particular difficulty with his evidence in chief being adduced in the format of the transcript of his testimony. But we did think it was an appropriate occasion to, as it were, draw the line in the sand. You may or may not have seen that during the course of proceedings today there has been a further motion suggesting the conversion, I think, of six witnesses from viva voce to 92 ter, and -- 12, sorry. 12. And the form of their evidence in chief varies greatly. And I think I speak for everybody when I say we would begin to, as it were, put down the marker and draw the line in the sand. Those witnesses, where the evidence in chief, it is proposed, will be in the form of an interview with investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor, and if the matter has to be addressed in more detail in writing or indeed orally, then it will be. And I'm getting ahead of everybody, really. In relation to that motion you likely to find that our response in relation to those who have been given evidence before, and have been cross-examined before, is that's fine. But in relation to people who have been through interviews which at varying times their status has changed and there have been breaks that have been referred to, you are likely to find that our stance will be that we would rather have their -- their evidence in chief received in the usual way. Not the least because we don't believe it will result in any saving of time. So the response in relation to the motion from yesterday, I think, is we have no difficulty with that. That witness can come 92 ter and the prior testimony can go in as evidence in chief in relation to the block booking, as it were, that's upcoming, you are likely to find a mixed response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. McCloskey, did you wish to address this matter? I think it has come --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can speak with Mr. Haynes about that to find out what his concerns are, given the latitude that is been given on cross-examination, I don't understand the foundation of the objection. We are of course willing to put witnesses on fully, I think the Court gets a better picture, but I think 92 ter has been working well, we have been able to save time, I don't see any prejudice with the right of -- the cross-examination that's being allowed. But given -- if there is a reason for any one or two particular witnesses, we might be able to -- or we can designate Mr. Ostojic to do the -- he can lead the witness as a cross-examination. I mean, I don't understand the foundation of that. But we'll talk with counsel about it and perhaps we can work something out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. At this stage we don't wish to comment on it. We leave it for the time being in your hands to discuss possibly and come to an agreement failing which of course we will need to intervene and decide. In the meantime, we are handing down an oral decision in the case of Witness number 154, pursuant to a Prosecution motion filed yesterday to convert this witness to a Rule 92 ter witness. Having heard the Prosecution submissions and those of the Defence, Prosecution motion is granted. And I hope Mr. McCloskey, that as indicated you will now proceed to disclose the 92 ter statement or statements to the Defence in a timely fashion so as to avoid unnecessary problems. Thank you. So we stand adjourned until tomorrow at 2.15. We will continue with the testimony of PW-104 and then we will see where we get after that. All right? Thank you.
